newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Alaska oil producers hope to slow decline.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Alaska oil producers hope to slow decline.

text.p: Alaska's oil producers are stepping up their spending next year as new discoveries and falling production costs offer new hope they can slow the decline in the state's once-bountiful fields.
Alaska's biggest producers, Atlantic Richfield Co and British Petroleum, recently announced multi-million dollar hikes in their yearly Alaskan budgets.
The increased spending comes despite an eight year fall in production of Alaskan North Slope (ANS) crude, which provides about 22 percent of total U.S. crude output.

Current production of ANS is down 500,000 barrels-per-day to 1.4 million from its peak in 1988, but new technology, such as directional drilling and three-dimensional seismic surveys, have helped locate new finds while cutting production costs by as much as 40 percent for companies like ARCO.

"I think it's a story now of a very healthy future for the industry in Alaska," John Morgan, president of BP Exploration Alaska Inc, said at a recent news conference announcing the firm's $1 billion boost in spending over the next five years.
A week before, ARCO pledged to add $500 million to its Alaska budget over the same period.
With costs down, ARCO is trying to develop these satellites and is predicting the 12 wells slated for 1997 development will add 5,000 to 10,000 bpd to its ANS output.
But satellites are just one part of ARCO's plans to offset declines in Alaska's Prudhoe Bay and Kuparuk regions.

Plans include pumping natural gas liquids (NGLs) from Prudhoe into Kuparuk to stimulate oil output, and developing Alpine, a new find near Prudhoe with an estimated 250 to 300 million barrels of oil. NGLs are often pumped into old wells to revive their flagging output.

"When we do all those things outside Prudhoe, our (ANS) decline per year will be about 6 percent," Thompson told Reuters, noting new projects will offset Prudhoe's current 12 percent annual rate of production declines.
Because of fields like Alpine, state officials have revised their production forecasts from last year.

"We're going to be producing a lot more oil around the turn of the century than we previously thought," Logsdon said. Since last year, he has raised his daily output forecast for the year 2000 to 1.288 million bpd -- up by 8,000 bpd.
Logsdon also raised his 2002 forecast by 90,000 bpd.
BP's expanded budget will develop new fields such as Northstar -- the first completely offshore ANS field with estimated reserves of 130 million barrels.
With Northstar and other finds, BP hopes to add four to five billion barrels to its production over the next decade.
State lawmakers hope development picks up after passing laws that allow oil companies to lower their royalty payments to Alaska's government, and by stream-lining leasing processes.
"It's intended to provide an incentive for development of marginal fields," said Bob King, press secretary to Alaska's Governor Tony Knowles, .
But opponents of the new laws see a darker side.

"The industry has used declining reserves to say we have to cut costs," such as environmental regulations, "but declines have been rather exaggerated." said Richard Fineberg, a consultant for the Northern Alaska Environmental Center and a former governor's aid.
One site whose development is hotly contested is the Artic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR).
"Politically that's going to be hard," said King, noting that President Clinton has opposed its development.
Company and state officials say a more tangible prospect is the Naval Petroleum Reserve-Alaska, a federally owned, 23 million acre site on the western border of the Alpine field.
"Now with fields immediately adjacent being developed with improved drilling and enhanced oil recovery, a lot of fields are worth a second look," said King.
Unlike ANWR, the Reserve has known reserves of about 2.1 billion barrels, and has been leased in the past.

King added it was too early to say if parts of Reserve would be leased this year, despite talks early this month in which Governor Knowles and U.S. Interior Secretary Bruce Babbit reportedly discussed that possibility.

"We think the area is prospective. We've seen new interest," ARCO's Thompson said. Thompson has said he thought recent finds like Alpine could serve as an example of how big oil could safely develop areas that are now off limits.
"Perhaps that could be a model to have them reconsider opening ANWR or the Naval Petroleum Reserve," Thompson said.
-- Los Angeles Bureau +213 380 2014
